source_text: Οὕτως ἡγητέον Σίμωνα τὸν μάγον ἀπεικάζοντας τῷ Λίβυϊ τάχιον ἀνθρώπῳ γενομένῳ οὕτως θεῷ. Εἰ δὲ ἔχει τὰ τῆς εἰκόνος ἀκριβῶς, καὶ πέπονθεν ὁ μάγος πάθος τι παραπλήσιον Ἀψέθῳ, ἐπιχειρήσωμεν μεταδιδάσκειν τοῦ Σίμωνος τοὺς ψιττακούς, ὅτι Χριστὸς οὐκ ἦν Σίμων ὁ ἑστώς, στάς, στησόμενος· ἀλλ᾿ ἄνθρωπος ἦν ἐκ σπέρματος, γέννημα γυναικός, ἐξ αἱμάτων καὶ ἐπιθυμίας σαρκικῆς καθάπερ καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ γεγεννημένος· καὶ ὅτι ταῦθ᾿ οὕτως ἔχει, προϊόντος τοῦ λόγου ῥᾳδίως ἐπιδείξομεν. Λέγει δὲ ὁ Σίμων μεταφράζων τὸν νόμον Μωϋσέως ἀνοήτως τε καὶ κακοτέχνως· Μωσέως γὰρ λέγοντος, ὅτι ὁ θεὸς πῦρ φλέγον ἐστὶ καὶ καταναλίσκον, δεξάμενος τὸ λεχθὲν ὑπὸ Μωσέως οὐκ ὀρθῶς, πῦρ εἶναι τῶν ὅλων λέγει τὴν ἀρχήν, οὐ νοήσας τὸ εἰρημένον, ὅτι θεὸς οὐ πῦρ, ἀλλὰ πῦρ φλέγον καὶ καταναλίσκον, οὐκ αὐτὸν διασπῶν μόνον τὸν νόμον Μωσέως, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸν σκοτεινὸν Ἡράκλειτον συλαγωγῶν. Ἀπέραντον δὲ εἶναι δύναμιν ὁ Σίμων προσαγορεύει τῶν ὅλων τὴν ἀρχήν, λέγων οὕτως· Τοῦτο τὸ γράμμα ἀποφάσεως φωνῆς καὶ ὀνόματος ἐξ ἐπινοίας τῆς μεγάλης δυνάμεως τῆς ἀπεράντου. Διὸ ἔσται ἐσφραγισμένον, κεκρυμμένον, κεκαλυμμένον, κείμενον ἐν τῷ οἰκητηρίῳ, οὖ ἡ ῥίζα τῶν ὅλων τεθεμελίωται. Οἰκητήριον δὲ λέγει εἶναι τὸν ἄνθρωπον τοῦτον τὸν ἐξ αἱμάτων γεγεννημένον, καὶ κατοικεῖν ἐν αὐτῷ τὴν ἀπέραντον δύναμιν, ἣν ῥίζαν εἶναι τῶν ὅλων φησίν. Ἔστι δὲ ἡ ἀπέραντος δύναμις, τὸ πῦρ, κατὰ τὸν Σίμωνα οὐδὲν ἁπλοῦν, καθάπερ οἱ πολλοὶ ἁπλᾶ λέγοντες εἶναι τὰ τέσσαρα στοιχεῖα καὶ τὸ πῦρ ἁπλοῦν εἶναι νενομίκασιν, ἀλλὰ γὰρ εἶναι τὴν τοῦ πυρὸς διπλῆν τινὰ τὴν φύσιν, καὶ τῆς διπλῆς ταύτης καλεῖ τὸ μέν τι κρυπτόν, τὸ δέ τι φανερόν· κεκρύφθαι δὲ τὰ κρυπτὰ ἐν τοῖς φανεροῖς τοῦ πυρός, καὶ τὰ φανερὰ τοῦ πυρὸς ὑπὸ τῶν κρυπτῶν γεγονέναι. Ἔστι δὲ τοῦτο, ὅπερ Ἀριστοτέλης δυνάμει καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ καλεῖ ἢ Πλάτων νοητὸν καὶ αἰσθητόν. Καὶ τὸ μὲν φανερὸν τοῦ πυρὸς πάντα ἔχει ἐν ἑαυτῷ ὅσα ἄν τις ἐπινοήσῃ ἢ καὶ λάθῃ παραλιπὼν τῶν ὁρατῶν. Τὸ δὲ κρυπτὸν πᾶν ὅ, τι ἐννοήσει τις νοητὸν καὶ πεφευγὸς τὴν αἴσθησιν ἢ καὶ παραλείπει μὴ διανοηθείς. Καθόλου δέ ἐστιν εἰπεῖν, πάντων τῶν ὄντων αἰσθητῶν τε καὶ νοητῶν, ὧν ἐκεῖνος κρυφίων καὶ φανερῶν προσαγορεύει, ἔστι θησαυρὸς τὸ πῦρ τὸ ὑπερουράνιον, οἱονεὶ δένδρον μέγα ὡς τὸ δι᾿ ὀνείρου βλεπόμενον τῷ Ναβουχοδονόσορ, ἐξ οὗ πᾶσα σὰρξ τρέφεται. Καὶ τὸ μὲν φανερὸν εἶναι τοῦ πυρὸς νομίζει τὸ πρέμνον, τοὺς κλάδους, τὰ φύλλα, τὸν ἔξωθεν αὐτῷ περικείμενον φλοιόν. Ἅπαντα, φησί, ταῦτα τοῦ μεγάλου δένδρου ἀναφθέντα ἀπὸ τῆς παμφάγου τοῦ πυρὸς ἀφανίζεται φλογός. Ὁ δὲ καρπὸς τοῦ δένδρου ἐὰν ἐξεικονισθῇ καὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ μορφὴν ἀπολάβῃ, εἰς ἀποθήκην τίθεται, οὐκ εἰς τὸ πῦρ. Γέγονε μὲν γὰρ, φησίν, ὁ καρπός, ἵνα εἰς τὴν ἀποθήκην τεθῇ, τὸ δὲ ἄχυρον, ἵνα παραδοθῇ τῷ πυρί, ὅπερ ἐστὶ πρέμνον, οὐκ αὐτοῦ χάριν ἀλλὰ τοῦ καρποῦ γεγενημένον.
pass_a_gloss: Thus Simon the magician should be considered as representing the Libyan quicker than a man who has become God. If indeed he has the things of the image accurately, and the magician suffered a passion similar to that of Apsethus, let us attempt to teach Simon's followers that Christ was not Simon who stood, stands, and will stand; but he was a man from seed, a offspring of a woman, born from blood and fleshly desire just like the rest; and that these things are so, we will easily show as the discourse proceeds. Simon says, translating the law of Moses foolishly and wickedly; for Moses said that God is a consuming fire, and having received what was said by Moses not correctly, he says that fire is the principle of all things, not understanding what was said, that God is not fire, but a consuming and destroying fire. Simon calls the principle of all things infinite power, saying: This letter is a declaration of voice and name from the great infinite power. Therefore, it will be sealed, hidden, and covered, lying in the dwelling place, where the root of all things is founded. He says that the dwelling place is this man born from blood, and the infinite power dwells in him, which he says is the root of all things. The infinite power is fire, according to Simon, not simple, as many say that the four elements and fire are simple, but it has a double nature, and of this double nature, he calls one part hidden and the other part visible; the hidden things are hidden in the visible things of fire, and the visible things of fire have been made by the hidden things. This is what Aristotle calls potential and actual, or what Plato calls intelligible and sensible. The visible part of fire has all things in itself, whatever one might think or even forget, leaving aside visible things. The hidden part is everything that one might think intelligibly and has escaped perception or has been left behind without being thought. In general, it is to be said that the fire is a treasure of all existing things, sensible and intelligible, which he calls hidden and visible; the heavenly fire is like a great tree, as seen in a dream by Nebuchadnezzar, from which all flesh is nourished. He thinks that the visible part of fire is the trunk, the branches, the leaves, and the bark that surrounds it on the outside. All these things, he says, of the great tree, having sprouted from the all-devouring fire, are destroyed by flame. But the fruit of the tree, if it is formed and has taken its own shape, is put into a storehouse, not into the fire. For the fruit, he says, was made to be put into the storehouse, but the chaff, to be given to the fire, which is the trunk, not made for its own sake, but for the sake of the fruit.

pass_b_english: We ought to regard Simon the Magician as representing the Libyan who became a god faster than any man. Indeed, if he truly bears the likeness, and if the magician has suffered a passion like that of Apsethus, then let us try to teach Simon's followers that Christ was not Simon, who stood, stands, and will stand; rather, he was a human being born from seed, the offspring of a woman, born of blood and fleshly desire just like everyone else. We will easily demonstrate these points as our discourse proceeds.

Simon claims to be translating the law of Moses, but he does so foolishly and wickedly. Moses declared that God is a consuming fire (Deuteronomy 4:24), yet Simon received this word incorrectly and teaches that fire itself is the first principle of all things. He failed to grasp that God is not fire, but a consuming and destroying fire. In doing so, he distorts not only the law of Moses but also plagiarizes the obscure Heraclitus.

Simon calls the first principle of all things 'infinite power,' and he declares: 'This letter is a declaration of voice and name from the great infinite power.' Therefore, it will be sealed, hidden, covered, and laid in the dwelling place where the root of all things is established. He identifies this dwelling place as the human being born from blood, saying that the infinite power — which he calls the root of all things — dwells within him.

According to Simon, this infinite power is fire, but it is not simple. Many suppose the four elements and fire itself are simple, but Simon insists that fire has a double nature. Of this double nature, he calls one part hidden and the other visible; the hidden things are concealed within the visible fire, and the visible fire has been produced by the hidden things. This distinction corresponds to what Aristotle calls potentiality and actuality, or what Plato calls the intelligible and the sensible.

The visible part of fire contains within itself everything one might conceive or even inadvertently overlook among visible things. The hidden part comprises everything one might grasp intellectually that has escaped perception or been passed over without being thought. In short, the heavenly fire is a treasury of all existing things — both sensible and intelligible — which Simon labels hidden and visible. It is like a great tree, such as Nebuchadnezzar saw in a dream, from which all flesh is nourished.

Simon says the visible fire corresponds to the trunk, the branches, the leaves, and the outer bark. All these parts of the great tree, having sprouted from the all-devouring fire, are consumed by flame. But the fruit of the tree, if it takes on its proper form and shape, is placed in a storehouse, not thrown into the fire. For the fruit, he says, was produced to be stored, while the chaff — which is the trunk — was produced not for its own sake but for the sake of the fruit.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological distinctions of Simonianism, including the dual nature of fire (hidden/visible), the Aristotelian/Platonic parallels, and the metaphor of the tree. Pass B correctly identifies and adds the scripture citation (Deuteronomy 4:24) for 'God is a consuming fire' which is required by the rules for added identifications. Pass A and B are consistent with the Greek.

Pass A: 'Simon the Magician' (Simon the Magician), 'the Libyan who became a god faster than any man' (Οὕτως ἡγητέον Σίμωνα τὸν μάγον ἀπεικάζοντας τῷ Λίβυϊ τάχιον ἀνθρώπῳ γενομένῳ οὕτως θεῷ). Pass B: 'God is a consuming fire (Deuteronomy 4:24)' (Μωσέως γὰρ λέγοντος, ὅτι ὁ θεὸς πῦρ φλέγον ἐστὶ καὶ καταναλίσκον).
